tldr: The authors proposed PolyMorph, a single reinforcement learning controller that can operate diverse legged robots with completely different leg counts and joint structures without any retraining—just by loading their URDF (robot description file).
hero_caption: An overview of PolyMorph. Diverse robots such as bipeds, tripeds, and quadrupeds are trained together in simulation (left), achieving zero-shot transfer to unseen morphologies and platforms (top right). Furthermore, it is deployed directly to real quadruped platforms (in regular quadruped, single-leg-locked triped, and front-legs-lifted biped configurations) to traverse rough terrain.
overview:
Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable results in legged robot locomotion, but traditional learned policies rely heavily on a specific robot morphology. When leg counts, joint structures, or mass distributions change, observation spaces, action spaces, and reward functions must be redesigned and retrained from scratch for each platform, incurring enormous engineering costs.

To solve this, the authors developed PolyMorph, a framework that directly reads joint-link connectivity extracted from the URDF and controls diverse legged robots with a single shared policy. It converts the robot structure into a graph representation, captures spatial dependencies using a Transformer, and summarizes past proprioception (joint angles, angular velocities, etc.) with a GRU, handling variable joint counts and different topologies.

What is also interesting about this work is that beyond model architecture, it systematizes practical techniques to eliminate 'learning bias' when training heterogeneous robots simultaneously. They introduced morphology-normalized rewards based on joint counts, adaptive sampling to focus on difficult bipeds, and a mechanism to automatically compute PD gains from the URDF's inertia matrix.

Simulation evaluations showed excellent tracking performance not only on trained robots spanning bipeds, tripeds, and quadrupeds, but also on unseen morphologies and platforms with drastically different masses. Furthermore, deploying the single policy directly onto real quadruped robots (Raibo1 and Raibo2) demonstrated stable outdoor rough-terrain traversal across normal quadruped, single-leg-locked triped, and upright biped modes.
contributions: Built a single URDF-conditioned policy architecture that can cross-control diverse legged robots with different joint counts, leg counts, and kinematic structures without retraining.

Solved reward scale mismatches, learning difficulty imbalances, and manual gain tuning burdens in heterogeneous multi-morphology RL using reward normalization, adaptive robot sampling, and URDF-derived automatic PD-gain calculation.

Evaluated generalization across numerous quadruped, triped, and biped robots as well as unseen platforms in simulation, and demonstrated outdoor rough-terrain locomotion across quadruped, triped, and biped configurations on real hardware using a single policy.

sections.heading: Can One Brain Control All Kinds of Robots?
sections.summary: Reinforcement learning for legged locomotion is powerful, but traditionally requires training an individual policy per robot. This paper proposes PolyMorph, which reads morphology information from a URDF to control robots with different leg and joint counts using a single policy.
sections.details:
Thanks to reinforcement learning (RL), quadruped robots can easily traverse steep slopes, stairs, and soft ground. This is because they can optimize tasks directly through trial and error with the environment without building accurate physics models like Model Predictive Control (MPC).

However, current legged robot learning has a major weakness: one policy is tied to one specific machine. If leg counts, link weights, or joint ordering change even slightly, observation spaces, action spaces, and reward functions must be rebuilt from scratch, requiring full retraining. This incurs massive time and effort whenever prototyping a new robot.

To tackle this, the authors asked: "Can we control a wide variety of legged robots with different leg counts and joint structures using just a single policy? And can we deploy it directly to real hardware without retraining?"

To make this possible, they proposed PolyMorph. It reads the robot's URDF file as a sequence of joint-link modules and adopts a network architecture that handles variable numbers of joints.

More importantly, they realized that changing the model architecture alone isn't enough for co-training multiple robots. Robots with more joints tend to incur larger reward penalties, and training tends to bias toward easily walkable platforms like quadrupeds, leaving bipedal locomotion behind. By incorporating practical techniques to resolve such training imbalances, PolyMorph achieves stable cross-embodiment control from simulation to real hardware.

sections.heading: Cross-Embodiment Controllers: How Does This Differ from Prior Work?
sections.summary: The authors organize prior work on Transformer-based robot control and cross-embodiment learning. PolyMorph's novelty lies in extending conventional structural priors and integrating a practical training pipeline to stably train heterogeneous morphologies simultaneously with RL.
sections.details:
Related work in robot control can be broadly divided into two streams:

### II-A Transformer Architectures for Robot Control
In RL policies, Transformers have primarily been used to process past sensor histories as temporal sequences. However, the Transformer's self-attention mechanism is also well suited for capturing spatial relationships between parts. Because input token length is flexible, it provides a natural framework for unifying robots with varying numbers of joints.
However, standard Transformers lack physical connectivity awareness, requiring them to learn from scratch which joint connects to which link, which hurts sample efficiency. Prior work like Body Transformer incorporated an adjacency graph as an attention mask for a single robot; PolyMorph extends this concept to a shared policy across heterogeneous morphologies.

### II-B Cross-Embodiment Learning
Many studies on controlling different platforms with a single policy have been proposed, such as Metamorph, GenLoco, URMA, and LocoFormer. These attempt to represent morphology via Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) or large-scale morphology randomization.
However, most prior works focused on model architecture and did not thoroughly address the collapse in learning dynamics when optimizing vastly different morphologies simultaneously with PPO (a representative RL algorithm). PolyMorph goes beyond network design to tackle training-level issues head-on, such as reward scale mismatches and sampling imbalances.

sections.heading: How PolyMorph Works: The URDF-Reading Brain and Training Secrets
sections.summary: PolyMorph consists of a GRU temporal encoder, a URDF-based graph-aware Transformer, and per-joint decoders. It also introduces morphology-normalized rewards, adaptive sampling, and URDF-derived automatic PD gains for stable co-training.
sections.details:
Figure F2 shows the overall architecture of PolyMorph. The control problem is formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), and a single shared policy $\pi_\theta$ is optimized across all robots using PPO.

### III-A State Context Encoder
Proprioceptive states—such as base roll-pitch, angular velocity, joint positions, velocities, and previous target positions—are fed into a shared GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit). Since robots have different joint counts, inputs are zero-padded to match the maximum number of joints ($N_{\max}=15$ in experiments). The GRU outputs a latent vector $\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{gru}}$ summarizing the temporal history, aiding balance recovery and disturbance rejection. An asymmetric Critic receives privileged information available only in simulation, such as base height, linear velocity, and terrain scan samples.

### III-B Morphology-Aware Transformer
The robot is represented as a sequence of modules, each consisting of a joint and its child link. Each token contains the link's mass, inertia, center of mass, and the joint's current position, reference position, history, and PD gains. Tokens are ordered from the kinematic tree root (base trunk) and zero-padded.
Crucially, the attention mechanism uses an attention bias $r$ derived from the URDF adjacency matrix $M$, masking out distant tokens so only physically connected modules interact strongly. This injects structural priors directly into the Transformer.

### III-C Decoder Network
The module features from the Transformer are concatenated with the GRU output $\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{gru}}$ and velocity command $\mathbf{o}_{cmd}$, then passed to the decoder. A per-joint decoder head outputs the mean of a Gaussian distribution to generate target joint angles. Non-actuated root modules and padding tokens are masked out from the actions.

### III-D Techniques for Stably Co-Training Diverse Robots
This is a major practical highlight:
- **Adaptive Robot Sampling**: Bipeds fall easily and are much harder to train than quadrupeds. With uniform environment allocation, quadrupeds master walking early while bipeds fail to learn. PolyMorph introduces a formula that increases sampling probability for robots with lower returns, concentrating computational resources on harder embodiments.
- **Reward Normalization**: Torque and acceleration penalties grow with joint count, while air time and foot clearance rewards depend on leg count. Dividing these by the number of active joints or legs eliminates reward scale disparities across platforms.
- **Automatic PD-gain Design**: Manually tuning PD gains for each robot is tedious. PolyMorph computes the overall robot inertia scale from the mass matrix $\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q}_0)$ in a nominal pose to determine $K_p$ with a common coefficient $\alpha=0.8$. It then sets $K_d$ to the median of critically damped gains derived from each joint's inertia and a damping ratio $\zeta=0.8$.

Right: fusing features with GRU temporal context and velocity commands to output per-joint target actions.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Conquering Unseen Robots and Injured Three-/Two-Legged Modes!
sections.summary: PolyMorph was trained on diverse robots in simulation, demonstrating generalization to unseen platforms and real-world deployment. Atlas (biped), which failed under uniform sampling, succeeded with adaptive sampling; real Raibo1 and Raibo2 conquered outdoor rough terrain in quadruped, triped, and biped modes.
sections.details:
Experiments used the RaiSim physics simulator, training for about 2.7 days (20,000 iterations) on an AMD EPYC CPU and NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. The deployed Actor network has only about 330k (0.33M) parameters, and on-board PC inference latency averaged 0.366 ms (running at 100 Hz).

### IV-A & B Framework Validation
The training set included Raibo1, Raibo2, Hound, Aliengo, Anymal-C, Atlas, Cassie, Go1, Laikago, Mini-Cheetah, and triped variants with one leg removed (FR, FL, HR, HL removed), spanning 11 kg to 135 kg.
- **Effects of Auto-Gains and Reward Normalization**: As shown in Table I, URDF-derived PD gains performed on par with manually tuned values. In Table II ablations, removing reward normalization widened reward gaps across robots, reduced final evaluation returns, and increased differences in terminal fall rates.
- **Power of Adaptive Sampling (Fig. F4)**: Under uniform sampling, the challenging biped Atlas suffered reward collapse mid-training and failed completely. Under adaptive sampling, Atlas was dynamically allocated more environments, achieving stable convergence just like the quadrupeds.
- **Outdoor Hardware Experiments (Fig. F3, Table III)**: Using real Raibo1 and Raibo2, the single policy traversed a 50 m outdoor course (pavement, slopes, stairs, grass) across normal quadruped, single-leg-locked triped, and front-legs-lifted biped modes—all without retraining. While tripeds occasionally caught their swing leg on steps, they exhibited robust traversal and recovery.

### IV-C & D Analysis & Baseline Comparisons
- **Velocity Command Tracking (Table IV)**: Testing zero-shot transfer on unseen quadrupeds B2 (70 kg) and Solo12 (2.5 kg). Even on B2, which exceeds the training mass range (11–52 kg), PolyMorph achieved low tracking RMSE comparable to seen robots. Solo12 had slightly lower precision due to its ultra-lightweight build (2.5 kg) but maintained locomotion without falling.
- **Latent Representation Visualization (Fig. F5)**: A t-SNE plot of Transformer morphology embeddings formed distinct clusters for bipeds, tripeds, and quadrupeds. Unseen robots landed near kinematically similar platforms, proving the network learns physical structure rather than memorizing robot IDs.
- **Baseline Comparisons (Fig. F6, Table V)**: PolyMorph outperformed an MLP baseline (PolyMorph-MLP) and prior methods Metamorph and URMA in total return across all robots. Lacking explicit structural bias and recurrent temporal processing, Metamorph and URMA destabilized as the curriculum progressed and failed on unseen platforms.

captions.F3: Outdoor deployment on real robots (Raibo1 and Raibo2). Using the same trained controller without retraining, the robots traverse grass, stairs, and curbs in regular quadruped mode, single-leg-locked triped mode, and standing biped mode.
captions.F4: Training curve comparison between adaptive sampling (left) and uniform sampling (right). Under uniform sampling, the difficult biped Atlas fails as its reward drops near zero. Adaptive sampling dynamically increases the environment count for Atlas, leading to stable convergence.
captions.F5: Left: Reward curves and terminal fall rates across robots. Right: t-SNE visualization of learned morphology token embeddings. Quadruped, triped, and biped clusters are cleanly separated, with structurally similar platforms grouped together.
captions.F6: Training curves compared against baseline methods. PolyMorph achieves the highest total return compared to PolyMorph-MLP, Metamorph, and URMA, maintaining high and balanced rewards across all morphologies without catastrophic collapse on specific robots.

sections.heading: Summary and Outlook: Toward True General-Purpose Legged Intelligence
sections.summary: PolyMorph shows that a single URDF-conditioned policy can control diverse legged robots. Future work aims to improve extrapolation to unseen morphologies with drastically different topologies.
sections.details:
This paper introduced PolyMorph, a morphology-conditioned framework that controls diverse legged robots with a single policy.

By processing URDF-derived joint-link modules using a graph-biased Transformer and a GRU, combined with morphology-normalized rewards, adaptive sampling, and automated PD-gain calculation, PolyMorph successfully co-trains quadrupeds, tripeds, and bipeds without destabilization. Demonstrating both simulation zero-shot generalization and real-robot deployment under locked-leg and biped configurations marks a very high level of completeness for robotics control research.

A current limitation noted by the authors is that while performance is robust within the training morphology distribution, it degrades on extreme extrapolation cases with drastically different skeletal topologies. Future work aims to introduce robot data augmentation through automatic URDF deformation and synthesis, exposing the policy to broader unseen morphologies during training to evolve into a foundation policy capable of walking any legged robot instantly.

takeaways: Beyond model architecture (Transformer + graph bias), stabilizing RL dynamics with reward normalization, adaptive sampling, and automatic PD-gain design is crucial for successful multi-morphology co-training.
Utilizing the URDF kinematic tree and mass matrix allows a unified pipeline that completely eliminates manual per-robot parameter tuning (such as gain adjustments).

Demonstrates immediate practical applicability for fault tolerance and morphology shifts—such as running a quadruped as a single-leg-locked triped or standing biped—using a single policy without retraining.
limitations: Tracking accuracy drops on robots with extreme mass scales or completely novel geometric topologies beyond the range covered in the training set.
Inherent kinematic constraints and limitations remain when forcing quadruped hardware into atypical configurations, such as insufficient swing-leg clearance causing trips in triped mode.
External vision sensors (exteroception) like cameras are not integrated; locomotion is limited to blind walking (proprioception only) in this paper.
